items.question: A freight-forwarding company runs a Claude step that routes inbound customer emails into 14 exception categories. Two of those categories — customs hold and damaged goods — are 3% of volume between them but account for almost all the operational cost of a misroute. The team is building a 400-item eval set from last quarter's 1.2 million emails. Which sampling approach best supports the decisions this eval has to inform?

options.A: Over-sample the two high-cost categories to a fixed quota, record the sampling weights, and report per-category and volume-weighted scores.
options.B: Sample the 400 emails the current router scored with the lowest routing confidence, since misroutes concentrate where the model is least certain.
options.C: Draw a uniform random sample of 400 emails across all 14 categories, so the headline accuracy is an unbiased estimate of production accuracy.
options.D: Take the 400 most recent emails from the end of the quarter, so the set reflects the newest customer phrasing and the seasonal exception mix.

items.question: In an eval suite, keeping a frozen holdout split that is never inspected during prompt iteration primarily protects against which failure?

options.A: Drift in the judge model's grading standard between releases as the judge prompt is revised.
options.B: Run-to-run variation in scores caused by sampling non-determinism in the model's outputs.
options.C: Label noise introduced by disagreement between the human annotators who wrote the references.
options.D: Reporting a score that reflects tuning to the specific eval items rather than task skill.

items.question: A streaming-media company compares two prompt variants for episode-summary generation using a pairwise LLM judge: the judge sees the transcript plus two candidate summaries labelled Summary 1 and Summary 2 and picks a winner. Variant B is always rendered second. Across 500 comparisons variant B wins 61%. Shipping B means retiring a prompt that three downstream teams depend on, so the eval lead wants to know how much of that margin is real before committing. What is the most direct way to find out?

options.A: Re-run all 500 comparisons with the presentation order swapped, and count only the pairs where the judge picks the same variant both times.
options.B: Add an explicit instruction to the judge prompt stating that presentation order is arbitrary and must not influence the verdict, then re-run.
options.C: Replace the pairwise protocol with independent absolute scoring of each summary against the rubric, and compare the two variants' mean scores.
options.D: Increase the comparison count from 500 to 2,000 so the interval around the 61% tightens and the margin is either confirmed or collapses.

items.question: A legal-services firm grades Claude-generated contract-clause summaries with an LLM judge on a 1–10 quality scale. In the release review, two reviewers looking at the same judge output disagree about whether a score of 7 means the summary is shippable to a client. Which changes to the grading design most directly resolve that disagreement? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Replace the 1–10 scale with a small number of levels, each carrying a written anchor and a worked example of what that level looks like.
options.B: Move the judge to the highest-capability model tier and re-grade the release sample, so the scores it emits are more reliable.
options.C: Have the judge answer the shipping question directly — whether the summary omits an obligation, deadline or party — rather than inferring it from a score.
options.D: Sample the judge five times per item and report the mean score to one decimal, so a single unlucky grade cannot move the verdict.
options.E: Have the judge emit the numeric score first and its written justification afterwards, so a long justification cannot drag the score around.

items.question: A hospital group extracts four fields from discharge summaries: medical record number, discharge date, primary ICD-10 diagnosis code, and a free-text follow-up instruction. The eval scores all four with case-insensitive exact match against a human-curated reference and reports one blended accuracy figure, currently 68%. Clinicians reviewing the same outputs say they would accept nearly all of them. What is the most likely explanation and the right correction?

options.A: The reference labels are stale relative to the current discharge-summary template; refresh them against recent charts and keep the single blended figure.
options.B: Exact match is too strict across the board; replace it with token-level F1 on all four fields so near-misses like a transposed digit get partial credit.
options.C: Output sampling is introducing variation; pin the generation settings so the four extracted strings stop drifting between runs of the same summary.
options.D: The free-text field has many correct phrasings; keep exact match on the three deterministic fields, rubric-grade the fourth, and report per-field results.

items.question: An insurance claims team wants to establish whether a redesigned prompt lifts first-pass accuracy from roughly 85% to roughly 90%. They plan a conventional two-sided test at the 5% level with 80% power, comparing two independently drawn samples of fresh claims. Their existing eval set holds 200 items. What does the arithmetic imply about this plan?

options.A: Around 100 items per arm is enough, since both proportions sit far from 50% where the variance of a proportion is at its maximum.
options.B: Sample size is not the binding constraint: with a fixed eval set both variants are scored on the same items, so the comparison is exact and no test applies.
options.C: 200 items per arm is adequate, because a 5-point difference is comfortably larger than the roughly ±3-point margin of error at that sample size.
options.D: They need on the order of 700 items per arm; at 200 the study is badly underpowered and a null result would carry almost no information.

items.question: Two annotators independently label the same 100 eval outputs pass or fail and agree on 94 of them. Which statistic reports how much of that agreement exceeds what random labelling with the same marginal rates would produce?

options.A: Cohen's kappa on the two annotators' pass/fail labels
options.B: Pearson correlation between the two annotators' label vectors
options.C: Raw percentage agreement over the 100 labelled items
options.D: F1 score, treating the first annotator's labels as ground truth

items.question: A tax-software company validates its LLM judge against human reviewers on a 100-item sample drawn at random from production. The judge and the humans each mark about 95 of the 100 outputs acceptable. Judge–human raw agreement is 94%, but Cohen's kappa comes out at 0.37. The plan was to sign off today and run the judge unsupervised over roughly 30,000 outputs a week. What should the team do next?

options.A: Build a second validation sample enriched with failing and borderline outputs, and re-measure agreement on the unacceptable class.
options.B: Sign off. 94% raw agreement on a randomly drawn production sample clears any reasonable bar for an unsupervised grader.
options.C: Shift the judge's decision threshold so it marks more outputs unacceptable, lifting kappa out of the fair range into substantial agreement.
options.D: Report Krippendorff's alpha in place of kappa, since it handles skewed label distributions without penalising genuinely high raw agreement.

items.question: A telco replaced the prompt behind its customer-support reply drafts. The offline LLM judge, which scores drafts against a five-criterion rubric, rates the new prompt materially higher. Six weeks after rollout, customer satisfaction and handle time are both flat. Someone notices the new prompt's replies average roughly three times the length of the old ones. Before rolling back or re-tuning, what is the most informative diagnostic to run?

options.A: Add a rubric criterion penalising any reply longer than a fixed word cap, then re-score both prompts and compare the adjusted totals.
options.B: Drop the offline judge and use customer satisfaction as the primary quality metric, since it reflects the outcome the business cares about.
options.C: Increase the judge samples per item from one to five and report the median, to rule out grading noise as the source of the apparent gain.
options.D: Plot judge score against reply length across both prompts, then re-score a length-matched subset to see whether the score gap survives.

items.question: An energy utility wants to retire the manual review step on its Claude-generated outage notifications and rely on an LLM judge to gate publication. The regulator expects the utility to be able to justify the change. Which pieces of evidence would actually establish that the judge can stand in for the human reviewers? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The judge attaching a self-reported confidence to each verdict, averaging above 0.9 across the full eval set.
options.B: Judge–human agreement on a sample enriched with the failure modes the reviewers currently catch, reported as a chance-corrected statistic.
options.C: Two independent runs of the same judge prompt at a fixed low temperature producing near-identical verdicts on every notification.
options.D: The judge and the human reviewers arriving at the same overall pass rate, within a point, across the full eval set.
options.E: Blind grading of outputs from both the incumbent and the candidate prompt, showing the judge's errors are not skewed toward either one.

items.question: A public-sector benefits agency uses a Claude step to flag applications for manual fraud investigation. Roughly 1.5% of applications are ultimately confirmed fraudulent, and the investigation team can work a bounded number of cases per week. The eval report currently leads with 98.7% overall accuracy and the programme board is satisfied. The eval lead is asked to make the report actually decision-useful. What should it lead with instead?

options.A: Overall accuracy with a 95% confidence interval and the sample size behind it, so the programme board can see how precisely the figure is estimated.
options.B: AUC-ROC, which is threshold-independent and therefore not distorted by the 1.5% confirmed-fraud base rate in the population.
options.C: Precision and recall on the fraud class at the operating threshold, plus the flag rate and the weekly caseload it implies for investigators.
options.D: Cohen's kappa between the model's flags and the investigators' final fraud determinations, as a chance-corrected agreement figure.

items.question: An eval task has a large space of equally acceptable outputs and no single reference answer. Which grading approach fits, and what does adopting it oblige you to build?

options.A: Model-graded rubric scoring, which obliges you to validate the grader against human judgements before its scores can be trusted.
options.B: Embedding similarity to a single chosen reference, which obliges you to select an embedding model and calibrate a cut-off.
options.C: Exact match against the modal human answer, which obliges you to collect several independent human answers per item first.
options.D: Human review of every item by a subject-matter expert, which obliges you to build no additional grading tooling or annotation guidelines.

items.question: A manufacturing company is starting a Claude feature that reads maintenance work orders and drafts parts-order requests for a planner to approve. The engineer proposes to build the prompt first, spend a week spot-checking outputs until it feels right, and then write an eval to lock the behaviour in. The tech lead pushes back. What is the strongest technical argument against the proposed ordering?

options.A: The eval must exist first so its items can be reused as the few-shot examples inside the prompt, keeping test cases and prompt in sync.
options.B: Without an eval the team cannot measure per-request latency and cost, and those are the constraints that will decide whether the feature ships.
options.C: Manual spot-checking is invalid because human reviewers cannot apply a quality standard consistently; only a model grader produces reproducible scores.
options.D: An eval written after the prompt codifies whatever the prompt already does, so it cannot say whether that behaviour clears the bar the business needs.

items.question: An ed-tech company has iterated its assignment-feedback prompt against the same 60-item eval set for four months. Pass rate on that set has climbed from 71% to 94% across about forty prompt revisions, each one made after reading the items that failed. Teacher complaints about unhelpful feedback have not moved over the same period. The team is preparing to present the 94% to their board. What should they do first?

options.A: Conclude that the eval measures a different construct than the teachers care about, and replace the metric with a teacher-satisfaction proxy scored by the judge.
options.B: Increase the judge samples per item and report the median pass rate, since the 23-point climb may be an artefact of grading variance.
options.C: Freeze the prompt and present the 94%; it is above the internal target, and further revisions at this point only add regression risk.
options.D: Draw a fresh sample from the same population, score the current prompt on it blind, and treat the gap between the two scores as the fitted share of the gain.

items.question: A retail marketplace evaluates generated product descriptions on a 4,000-item suite. Generation runs on a cheaper tier; grading uses a rubric judge on the highest tier, and grading now costs several times more than generation on every run, which the team performs before each prompt change. The eval lead must cut grading spend without losing the ability to detect a two-point change in pass rate. What is the soundest redesign?

options.A: Reduce the suite to the 1,000 items the current prompt most often fails, since items that already pass carry no information about further improvement.
options.B: Move the rubric judge down to the generation tier and accept noisier grades, since random error averages out across 4,000 items.
options.C: Run deterministic checks first — schema validity, banned terms, attribute coverage — count those failures in code and send only the survivors to the judge.
options.D: Grade a random 400-item subsample on each run and extrapolate its pass rate to the full 4,000-item suite, refreshing the subsample each run.

items.question: A permitting agency evaluated two prompt variants over the same 300 eval items, but analysed each as an independent proportion. Variant A scored 82.0% (95% CI 77.6–86.4) and variant B scored 85.7% (95% CI 81.7–89.7). Variant B costs about 40% more per request because it uses a higher model tier. The intervals overlap, and the delivery lead has concluded there is no evidence of a difference. What should the eval lead do next?

options.A: Re-analyse the existing results as a paired comparison over the shared items, testing only the items where the two variants disagree.
options.B: Accept the delivery lead's reading and keep variant A, since overlapping 95% intervals mean the difference is not statistically significant.
options.C: Ship variant B, since a 3.7-point gain measured over 300 items is a large enough effect to justify the 40% higher per-request cost.
options.D: Expand the suite from 300 to 1,200 items and re-run both variants as independent samples, halving each interval's width.

items.question: An airline's eval team must be able to detect a three-point change in pass rate on a rebooking-explanation task. The item count is capped by the annotation budget and cannot grow this quarter. Which changes reduce the variance of the estimated difference between two prompt variants, given that constraint? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Generate several outputs per item per variant and score the best one, so each variant is represented by its strongest response.
options.B: Relax the two-sided significance level from 0.05 to 0.10, so a smaller observed difference clears the threshold.
options.C: Run both variants over the identical item set and analyse the outcomes as paired rather than as two independent proportions.
options.D: Grade each item several times with the judge and take the majority verdict as that item's recorded outcome.
options.E: Report the difference with a bootstrap confidence interval resampled over items rather than a normal approximation.

items.question: A grading rubric is rewritten to decompose quality into five independent binary criteria rather than one 1–5 overall quality score. What does that buy, and what does it cost?

options.A: It removes the need to validate the grader against human labels, because binary criteria are objective checks rather than judgement calls.
options.B: It attributes each failure to a named criterion and raises rater agreement, at the cost of needing a rule for how the five combine into a ship decision.
options.C: It guarantees higher agreement with human reviewers on every criterion, at the cost of substantially more judge tokens per graded item.
options.D: It makes scores directly comparable across different grading tasks, at the cost of losing the ability to represent partial quality.

items.question: A research-publishing platform is deciding whether to keep its in-house abstract-generation prompt or license a third-party service. The bake-off uses a pairwise LLM judge over 300 papers; the in-house output, produced by the same model family the judge runs on, wins 68%. A reviewer on the architecture board points out that the judge and one of the candidates share a model family and asks whether the result can be relied on. What is the right response?

options.A: Extend the bake-off from 300 to 1,200 papers so the interval around the 68% win rate is tight enough to settle the reviewer's question outright.
options.B: Tell the judge in its prompt which abstract came from its own model family and instruct it to compensate for any preference it may hold.
options.C: Validate the verdicts against a blind human-labelled subsample and a judge from another model family, reporting both alongside the win rate.
options.D: Switch from pairwise comparison to independent rubric scoring of each abstract, which removes any preference between the two candidates.

items.question: A safety check ran against 300 independently sampled eval items and produced zero failures. Approximately what can be claimed about the true failure rate at 95% confidence?

options.A: The rate is zero: 300 clean draws demonstrate the check is reliable on this task.
options.B: The rate is no higher than roughly 1%, that is one failure per hundred requests.
options.C: The rate is no higher than roughly 0.3%, one failure across the 300 items sampled.
options.D: No bound can be computed, since at least one observed event is required to estimate a rate.

items.question: A mining-equipment supplier is building the first eval for a field-service assistant that answers technicians' questions about breakdown procedures. Only 40 real transcripts survived the last CRM migration, so an engineer generates 500 synthetic transcripts with Claude and labels those. The suite is due to become the ship gate for the pilot. What is the principal risk, and what control should accompany the synthetic set?

options.A: Generating 500 transcripts consumes tokens the pilot budget did not plan for; cap the set at 200 items and expand it once the pilot has proved out.
options.B: Synthetic transcripts may reproduce technicians' personal data from the 40 real seeds; run a redaction pass over the whole set before any labelling begins.
options.C: Generated cases skew hard, because a model asked for examples produces edge cases; balance the set with routine breakdown queries so the pass rate is not depressed.
options.D: Synthetic transcripts inherit the model's idea of the task, so the suite can pass while real traffic fails; keep the 40 real ones as an anchor that scores must track.

items.question: A ticketing company built a 600-item eval set by harvesting questions from its help-centre knowledge base. During a review someone notices that about 180 of the items are paraphrases of just 12 underlying questions, because those articles have many indexed variants. The team reports a pass rate with a confidence interval computed at n = 600. What is the consequence and the right correction?

options.A: The effective sample is well below 600, so the interval is too narrow; cap paraphrases per underlying intent and spend the freed budget on uncovered intents.
options.B: Paraphrase clusters are a strength, because they measure robustness to phrasing; keep the clusters and replace the pass rate with a per-cluster consistency metric.
options.C: The duplication is harmless as long as each item's label is correct, since the judge grades every one of the 600 items independently of the others.
options.D: Delete all 180 paraphrased items and report on the remaining 420, since near-duplicates of any kind invalidate a reference set.

items.question: A grocery retailer's eval report breaks a substitution-suggestion task into 20 slices by product category. A prompt change moves the overall pass rate by an amount well inside the noise, but one slice — frozen foods — shows an improvement significant at p = 0.04. The product manager wants to ship the change for frozen foods and cites the p-value. How should the eval lead handle this?

options.A: Accept the frozen-foods finding as confirmed; it cleared the conventional 0.05 threshold on a pre-existing slice of the standard report.
options.B: Grow the eval set until every one of the 20 category slices is individually powered to significance, then re-read the report.
options.C: Stop reporting slice-level results altogether and publish only the overall pass rate, since slicing the report into 20 categories is what manufactured the finding.
options.D: Apply a multiplicity correction across the 20 slices, note that about one is expected to clear 0.05 by chance, and re-test frozen foods on a fresh sample.

items.question: An eval must be reproducible: re-running the same suite against the same prompt should produce the same graded outcome. What does configuring the judge's sampling to be effectively deterministic achieve, and what does it leave in place?

options.A: It removes disagreement between the judge and the human labels it was validated against, though not the variation between judge runs.
options.B: It largely removes run-to-run variation in the grade, but leaves untouched any systematic error in the standard the judge applies.
options.C: It removes both run-to-run variation and any preference tied to the order and formatting in which candidates are presented.
options.D: It achieves nothing useful, because a language model's token sampling cannot be made reproducible in any meaningful sense.

items.question: A games studio is running a human preference eval to choose between two prompt variants for non-player-character dialogue. Six internal raters will each see the two outputs for a set of scenes and pick the one they prefer. The studio intends to use the result to justify a change that affects three shipped titles. Which controls belong in the protocol? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Show raters the current pass rate on the existing eval suite before they start, so they can calibrate their strictness.
options.B: Randomise which variant appears first for each scene, and record the assignment so the effect of order can be checked afterwards.
options.C: Recruit the six raters from the prompt-engineering team, since they understand the intended dialogue behaviour best.
options.D: Withhold from raters which variant produced which output, and keep the mapping outside the rating interface throughout.
options.E: Discard any scene where the six raters split three–three, since an even split carries no usable preference signal.

items.question: A waste-management operator uses a Claude step to read sensor-fault descriptions and decide whether to auto-dispatch a technician or queue the case for human triage. Finance has costed the two errors: an unnecessary dispatch costs about £400, and a genuine fault left in the queue costs about £6,000 in vehicle downtime. The data-science team currently sets the decision threshold at the point that maximises F1 on the eval set. What should determine the threshold instead?

options.A: Sweep the threshold and pick the point minimising expected cost under the 15-to-1 error ratio, then report precision, recall and dispatch volume.
options.B: Keep the F1-maximising threshold, since the harmonic mean of precision and recall already balances the two error types against each other.
options.C: Maximise recall on genuine faults, since the £6,000 downtime event is the expensive error and each miss costs fifteen unnecessary dispatches.
options.D: Set the threshold so the weekly auto-dispatch volume exactly matches the technician crew's current capacity, and hold it there.

items.question: An agricultural co-operative's Claude step drafts pesticide-application advisories from field reports for an agronomist to sign off. The current eval run covers 4,000 items and the pass rate is 76%, giving 960 failures. The team has one two-week improvement sprint funded before the season starts, and the graded output carries nothing but a pass or fail per item. What should they do first?

options.A: Start with the failures the judge scored lowest, since those are the worst outputs and fixing them gives the biggest quality lift per item.
options.B: Sample 100 of the 960 failures at random and revise the prompt to handle each one in turn until the two-week sprint runs out.
options.C: Hand-code a sample of failures into mutually exclusive categories, size each against the 960, and pick the target by frequency times consequence.
options.D: Re-run the 960 failures on a higher model tier and take the proportion that resolve as the estimate of achievable improvement this sprint.

items.question: A law firm's eval set for a clause-extraction task holds 400 items built from 25 source contracts, sixteen questions per contract. The report gives a pass rate with a 95% interval computed at n = 400, and the partner sponsoring the project is being asked to accept that interval as the basis for a go-live decision. Which criticism is correct, and what should change?

options.A: Compute the interval at n = 400 as now, but widen it by a fixed factor of two as a conservative allowance for correlation between items from one contract.
options.B: Treat the contract as the sampling unit: build the interval by resampling contracts, and spend future budget on more contracts rather than more questions each.
options.C: Average the sixteen items in each contract into one score and report the mean of the 25 contract scores without an interval, since 25 is too few for inference.
options.D: Keep n = 400; item-level independence holds because each of the sixteen questions asks about a different clause and is graded on its own rubric.

items.question: A code-generation eval reports pass@5. What does that figure support about a production system that returns one generated answer to the user?

options.A: It supports the claim directly, since pass@5 is an unbiased estimate of the probability that the model can solve the task at all.
options.B: It supports the claim once divided by five, an adjustment that discounts the metric for the four extra attempts it allows.
options.C: It supports the claim provided the eval also reports the pass@5 figure under a fixed random seed and a pinned model version, so every run reproduces exactly.
options.D: Very little: pass@5 is the chance one of five samples is correct, overstating single-shot behaviour unless production samples five and selects correctly.

items.question: A media-monitoring company is labelling a 1,000-item golden set for sentiment-toward-brand in news coverage. Three annotators have completed a first 120-item batch; Cohen's kappa between pairs sits around 0.41, and the disagreements cluster on articles that mention the brand only in passing. The set is meant to become the reference for validating an LLM judge. Which steps will most improve the quality of these labels? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Write a labelling guide that states the decision rule for the specific cases the annotators are disagreeing on, with a worked example of each edge case.
options.B: Increase the annotator pool from three to eight and take the majority label on each article, since more independent votes reduce labelling noise.
options.C: Run a calibration round on a shared batch, work through the disagreements together, revise the guide, and re-measure kappa before labelling continues.
options.D: Replace the three human annotators with an LLM labeller, which will at least apply one consistent standard across all 1,000 items.
options.E: Route remaining disagreements to a named adjudicator whose decision is recorded with its reason, so every golden label carries provenance.

items.question: To build a 500-item golden set for rights-clearance summaries quickly, an analyst at a book publisher had Claude draft the reference answer for each item and then reviewed each one to approve or edit it. Eighty-four percent were approved with no edit. The production prompt, running on the same model tier, now scores 91% against that set, and the team is preparing to use the score as the pilot's acceptance evidence. What is the problem?

options.A: Nothing structural. Model-drafted references with human approval is standard practice, and an 84% unedited approval rate indicates the drafts were of high quality.
options.B: The set is too easy for the current system; add harder rights-clearance items until the score falls into a range that discriminates between prompt versions.
options.C: References produced by the system under test make the eval partly a self-consistency check; independently re-author a subset and compare the two subsets' scores.
options.D: A single approver produces no inter-rater agreement statistic, so all 500 labels are unaudited and no score computed against them can be trusted.

items.question: A car manufacturer's owner's-manual assistant is evaluated with a single headline score defined as 0.5 × factual accuracy + 0.3 × tone + 0.2 × conciseness, each component a pass rate on its own rubric. Over two quarters the headline score rose from 0.79 to 0.84 while factual accuracy fell from 0.88 to 0.83. Product leadership has been tracking only the headline. Which statements about this design are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: A linear weighted composite lets one component be paid for by gains in the others, so the headline can rise while the highest-consequence component falls.
options.B: Normalising the three components to z-scores over the quarter's items before weighting them would remove the substitution effect.
options.C: Re-deriving the weights each quarter from a regression of the headline on downstream user outcomes would prevent component substitution.
options.D: Publishing the three components with the headline and imposing a floor on factual accuracy that no gain elsewhere can offset makes the trade visible and blocks it.
options.E: The underlying error is that conciseness at 0.2 carries too much weight relative to accuracy at 0.5; correcting the weights resolves it.

items.question: An eval needs to confirm that generated output conforms to a required JSON schema. Which grading approach is appropriate, and what does it leave unmeasured?

options.A: Programmatic schema validation, which is exact and cheap but says nothing about whether the field values are correct.
options.B: A model grader asked whether the output looks like valid JSON, which copes better with malformed output than a parser would.
options.C: Exact string match against a reference JSON document, which covers structure and values in a single check.
options.D: Embedding similarity between the generated object and a reference object, which tolerates differences in key ordering.

items.question: A five-criterion judging rubric includes both "is the answer complete" and "does the answer omit any required element", and the item's score is the count of criteria passed. What is the practical consequence?

options.A: None worth acting on: the two criteria agreeing on nearly every item confirms the judge is applying the rubric consistently across the whole item set.
options.B: Grading cost rises because the judge produces two verdicts where one would do, with no change to the information the score carries.
options.C: One underlying defect is counted twice, so an omission costs twice as much as an unrelated defect and the criteria stop being independent evidence.
options.D: The two criteria will diverge on borderline items, which is useful because that divergence flags the items that need human review.

items.question: After an incident, a pharmacy chain estimates that a specific failure mode in its medication-interaction summarisation step occurs in roughly one request in five hundred. Regulatory sign-off requires a fresh randomly sampled eval run in which the team can state that the failure mode was very likely to have been exercised at least once. Annotation is the binding cost. Roughly how large should the sample be?

options.A: About 500 items, since exactly one occurrence is expected at that size and that makes detection likely.
options.B: About 200 items reviewed at high scrutiny, since for rare failures review depth matters more than sample size.
options.C: About 5,000 items, because rare-event detection needs an order of magnitude beyond the reciprocal of the rate.
options.D: About 1,500 randomly sampled items, roughly three times the reciprocal of the one-in-five-hundred rate.

items.question: An HR-tech company tracks a quarterly pass-rate trend for its interview-summary feature, sourced from an eval set that engineers edit in place as they add cases. Last month someone removed 30 items they judged unrealistic. The trend chart shows a four-point jump in the same period, and nobody can now say whether the jump came from a prompt change or from the removal. Which practices would have prevented the ambiguity? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Keep the eval set in the same repository as the prompt so the two always change together in a single reviewed commit.
options.B: Treat each eval set state as an immutable versioned artefact and stamp its version on every score, so two versions are never silently compared.
options.C: Rescale historical scores to the new item count whenever items are removed, so the quarterly trend line stays continuous.
options.D: Freeze the eval set permanently at its first version, since any subsequent addition or removal makes the trend uninterpretable.
options.E: Require every item removal to carry a recorded reason and to be applied as a new set version rather than an in-place edit.

items.question: A national parks agency is starting work on a Claude step that drafts replies to public consultation submissions. Today two policy officers write every reply by hand. The delivery team wants to begin prompt engineering this week and has asked the eval lead to nominate an acceptance threshold. What should the eval lead do before nominating a number?

options.A: Measure the existing manual process on the same items — officer throughput, and how often two officers independently rate the same draft acceptable.
options.B: Set the bar at 95% acceptable, which is the standard the agency already applies to the published correspondence it sends under its own name.
options.C: Build the first stable prompt version, see where it lands on the eval, and adopt that score as the baseline for every later version to improve on.
options.D: Decline to set a numeric bar and rely on officer sign-off of every draft during the pilot, deferring the eval until volumes make automation worthwhile.

items.question: A subtitling company grades Spanish subtitle translations with an LLM judge that sees the English source and the candidate translation and returns a 1–5 quality rating. Reviewers report that the judge rates almost everything 4 or 5, including segments where a domain specialist can point at a clear meaning error. The company has a library of professionally produced reference translations for a subset of its catalogue. What change to the grading design would most improve discrimination?

options.A: Widen the rating scale from 1–5 to 1–10, giving the judge more room to separate the many segments it currently rates 4 or 5 alike.
options.B: Supply the professional reference alongside the source and candidate, and require the judge to name meaning divergences before it rates.
options.C: Replace the judge with an n-gram overlap score against the professional reference translation, which is objective, cheap and fully reproducible.
options.D: Keep the reference-free setup but decompose the 1–5 rating into three sub-dimensions — accuracy, fluency and timing — and sum them.

items.question: A pharmaceutical company's medical-information team must choose between two prompt versions for drafting responses to healthcare-professional enquiries. Both are graded with a four-level absolute rubric, and across 500 items both land on the same level for 96% of items, giving effectively identical scores. The team's own reviewers, reading a handful side by side, consistently prefer one version. The decision has to be defended to a governance committee. What should the eval lead do?

options.A: Grade each output five times with the same four-level rubric and average, so the discrete levels become a finer-grained continuous score.
options.B: Widen the absolute rubric from four levels to ten, giving the small differences between the two versions somewhere to land.
options.C: Present the two outputs for each item side by side with the order randomised, and report the win, tie and loss distribution across the 500 items.
options.D: Conclude the versions are equivalent on quality and decide on cost, since a rubric that cannot separate them is evidence there is nothing to separate.

items.question: A European rail operator runs a Claude-based passenger enquiry assistant in four languages. English is 71% of traffic, German 18%, French 7% and Dutch 4%. The overall eval pass rate has held steady at 89% across the last two releases, but complaints from Dutch-speaking passengers have roughly tripled since the most recent one. The eval lead is asked why the suite did not catch it. What is the correct change to the eval design?

options.A: Keep the aggregate as the headline and handle the complaints as a support issue, since they are not yet corroborated by any eval measurement.
options.B: Increase the overall eval set size until the aggregate pass rate is sensitive enough to register a regression in a single language.
options.C: Add a language-quality criterion to the judging rubric, so the aggregate pass rate falls whenever the output in any of the four languages degrades.
options.D: Report the pass rate per language cohort with its own interval, sizing each cohort to detect a meaningful move rather than to match traffic share.

items.question: What property most distinguishes a golden dataset from any other collection of eval items?

options.A: It is larger than the working eval set, which is what allows the narrower confidence intervals quoted on the reported score.
options.B: It is constructed to cover the edge cases and adversarial inputs a system has not yet encountered in production traffic.
options.C: Its labels are established independently of the system under test and treated as authoritative, so any disagreement is a system error.
options.D: It is refreshed at every release so that it always reflects the current production traffic distribution and item mix.

items.question: A professional-services firm has reported a monthly quality trend for its engagement-summary feature for two years, graded by a judge pinned to one model version. The firm's own model-lifecycle policy now requires that pin to be replaced. On a trial run over the identical items with the identical system prompt, the new judge returns a pass rate six points higher. The trend chart is reviewed by the firm's risk committee. How should the migration be handled?

options.A: Adopt the new figure and annotate the chart with the migration date; the newer judge is more capable, so its grades are the more accurate of the two.
options.B: Score a stored corpus with both judges, quantify the offset by item type, re-validate the new judge against human labels, and re-baseline the trend.
options.C: Adjust the new judge's rubric wording until it reproduces the old judge's pass rate on the same items, so the trend line remains continuous.
options.D: Keep the old judge pinned indefinitely, since a stable measurement serves the risk committee better than a current one does.

items.question: What does a bootstrap confidence interval on an eval metric give you that a normal-approximation interval may not?

options.A: A systematically narrower interval, because resampling extracts more information out of the same set of graded items.
options.B: Protection against a biased grader, because resampling averages the grader's individual errors out across many replicates.
options.C: A correct interval even when the eval items are correlated, because resampling automatically preserves the correlation structure in the graded data.
options.D: An interval for statistics whose sampling distribution is not near normal — medians, ratios, composites — with no closed-form standard error.

items.question: An internal audit of a government department's AI register finds that a pass rate quoted in a ministerial briefing six months ago cannot be reproduced. The eval pipeline stored the resulting score and nothing else. Which records would have made that run reproducible? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The eval set version identifier and the exact list of item ids scored in the run.
options.B: The names of the engineers who reviewed the run output before it was quoted.
options.C: The prompt version, model identifier and generation settings used to produce the outputs.
options.D: The judge prompt version, judge model identifier and grading settings used to score them.
options.E: The wall-clock duration of the run and the total token spend it incurred.

items.question: A defence-electronics manufacturer is designing the eval for a Claude step that turns engineering specifications into technician test-procedure checklists. The eval budget allows a rubric judge on every item. For which of these grading needs is a model judge the wrong instrument? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Deciding whether the ordering of steps in the checklist is logically coherent given the dependencies in the specification.
options.B: Confirming that every part number cited in the checklist exists in the manufacturer's parts master file.
options.C: Judging whether the wording of each step is clear enough for a technician with roughly two years' experience.
options.D: Assessing whether a safety caveat that the specification implies but does not state explicitly has been included.
options.E: Verifying that the checklist's stated total duration equals the sum of the durations it gives for the individual steps.

items.question: A cosmetics retailer's ingredient-question assistant scores 99% on its 250-item eval suite and has done so for the last five releases. Over the same period the customer-support team has escalated a steady stream of incorrect allergen answers, none of which resemble anything in the suite. The eval currently gates release. What should the team do next?

options.A: Treat the suite as saturated: source new items from the escalations and uncovered traffic, and check they separate two prompt versions before gating.
options.B: Tighten the judge's rubric on the existing 250 items until the pass rate falls back into a range where release-to-release movement is clearly visible.
options.C: Continue reporting the 99% and route the allergen escalations into a separate manual quality process, since the two measure different things.
options.D: Reduce the suite to the handful of items that still fail occasionally, so the reported pass rate has room to move between releases.

items.question: For evaluating abstractive summaries against a single human reference summary, what is the central limitation of n-gram overlap metrics such as ROUGE?

options.A: They are too expensive to run over a large eval set, because the overlap computation is quadratic in the summary length.
options.B: They cannot be computed at all when the candidate summary is longer than either the reference summary or the source document.
options.C: They measure surface word overlap, so a faithful paraphrase scores low while an unfaithful copy of the reference's wording scores high.
options.D: They are undefined for candidates shorter than the reference summary, which systematically biases the metric against concise output.

items.question: A credit union wants to replace its manual quality sampling of member-message drafts with an LLM judge. Its risk function will accept the change only if the team can state judge–human agreement to within about ±5 percentage points at 95% confidence. Roughly 8% of drafts currently fail manual QA. Human labelling is the binding cost. What does this require?

options.A: Around 400 human-labelled items, which is what a ±5-point interval on a proportion needs, drawn so that enough of them are failures.
options.B: Around 100 human-labelled items, since agreement is expected to be high and proportions near 1 have lower variance than proportions near 0.5.
options.C: Around 1,500 human-labelled items, matching the size of the main eval run so that the two figures are directly comparable to one another.
options.D: Sample size is not the binding constraint: label any convenient number with two humans as well, since human–human agreement bounds judge–human agreement.

items.question: A water utility's leak-report triage assistant is evaluated with a suite that reports one pass rate per run. Re-running the identical suite against the identical prompt on three consecutive occasions returned 84%, 87% and 82%. The board's quarterly pack shows only the most recent figure, and last quarter's pack showed 82%. Which changes make the reported number defensible? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Run the suite several times per configuration and report the mean with its spread, so readers can separate a real move from run-to-run noise.
options.B: Report the highest of the three runs, on the grounds that it represents what the system has demonstrably shown it can do.
options.C: Restrict the suite to the items whose outcome is stable across repeated runs, so the reported quarterly figure stops moving.
options.D: Reduce generation variability where the configuration allows it, and state the sampling settings used alongside the score.
options.E: Grow the eval set until the run-to-run spread disappears entirely, which removes the need to report variability at all.

items.question: Some eval pipelines include a small number of deliberately defective outputs whose correct grade is known in advance, scored on every run alongside the real ones. What does that add?

options.A: It raises the overall difficulty of the suite so that the headline pass rate lands in a more discriminating range between releases.
options.B: It is a standing check on the grader: if the judge passes an output built to violate a named criterion, the grading pipeline is broken.
options.C: It supplies negative examples the prompt can be tuned against, improving the system's handling of similar cases in production traffic.
options.D: It establishes the empirical floor of the achievable score range, so the reported pass rate can be normalised against that floor.

items.question: A veterinary telemedicine platform's Claude step returns a triage recommendation together with a stated confidence of high, medium or low. The routing logic sends every low-confidence case to a duty vet and auto-sends the rest. The current eval reports only overall recommendation accuracy, and it is 91%. Which statements about what this eval is failing to measure are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Confidence can be evaluated by checking that the model reports high confidence on the large majority of cases, since a good system should mostly be confident.
options.B: Because the confidence is self-reported by the model, it cannot be evaluated, and the routing logic should be driven by a separately trained classifier instead.
options.C: The routing depends entirely on whether accuracy at high confidence genuinely exceeds accuracy at low confidence, so the eval must report accuracy per level.
options.D: Overall accuracy already accounts for the confidence signal, because miscalibrated confidence would show up as a lower overall accuracy figure on the eval.
options.E: A system can be well calibrated and inaccurate, or accurate and badly calibrated; since routing consumes the confidence, calibration needs its own metric and threshold.

items.question: An eval's acceptance threshold — the score at which a version is permitted to ship — should be derived principally from what?

options.A: The score the current production version achieves on the same suite, so that no release ever ships worse than the incumbent does.
options.B: A conventional level such as 90%, adjusted upward or downward according to how difficult the task is judged to be.
options.C: The highest score any candidate version has achieved so far, so that the bar ratchets upward as the system improves.
options.D: The consequence of the residual errors at that score: what the failures cost, who absorbs them, and which control catches them.

items.question: A parcel carrier's address-normalisation eval runs two graders over every item: a deterministic check that validates the returned postcode against the national address file, and a rubric judge that assesses whether the normalised address is usable for delivery. On 8% of items the deterministic check fails while the judge passes. The suite currently reports the judge's pass rate as the headline. What should the eval lead do next?

options.A: Treat the deterministic check as authoritative for the postcode, then hand-review a sample of the judge's passes on those items to find the cause.
options.B: Take the disjunction and pass an item if either grader passes it, since requiring both to agree imposes a stricter bar than the delivery task needs.
options.C: Remove the deterministic check, since the rubric judge already assesses deliverability and two overlapping graders create the double-counting problem.
options.D: Take the conjunction of the two graders, report the lower combined number, and treat the disputed 8% as failures without investigating.

items.question: An eval covers ten task categories of very unequal size. What distinguishes a macro-average from a micro-average of the per-category results, and when does the choice matter?

options.A: Macro-averaging weights each item equally and micro-averaging weights each category equally; the two diverge only when the categories differ in pass rate.
options.B: Macro-averaging weights each category equally and micro-averaging weights each item equally, so they diverge when small and large categories differ.
options.C: The two are equivalent for a simple pass rate and differ only for precision and recall, where the denominators are class-conditional.
options.D: Micro-averaging should be used for eval reporting in all cases, because it is the unbiased estimate of performance on live production traffic.

items.question: A children's education platform runs a Claude-based homework assistant that must decline to write a student's essay for them but must still explain concepts, critique a student's own draft, and answer factual questions. The eval reports a single number: an inappropriate-completion rate of 0.4% on a 2,000-item set of requests that should be declined. Teachers have started complaining that the assistant refuses ordinary help requests. What must be added to the measurement design? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Triple the decline set so the 0.4% figure has a tighter interval, since inappropriate completions are the only outcome that carries real risk.
options.B: Measure an unnecessary-refusal rate on a separate set of requests that should be answered, since tightening the boundary raises refusals of legitimate work.
options.C: Replace the pass/fail verdict on completions with a severity-weighted score, so borderline cases contribute less than clear-cut violations.
options.D: Define a joint acceptance criterion in which neither rate may worsen, so no prompt change can trade one against the other unnoticed at the gate.
options.E: Combine both behaviours into one weighted policy-adherence rate so the team has a single number to track, report and set a target on.

items.question: In a comparison of two candidate versions of a system over a shared eval set, which items contribute nothing to distinguishing the two versions?

options.A: Items whose reference answer was written by a single annotator with no adjudication round.
options.B: Items that both versions answer correctly, and items on which both versions fail.
options.C: Items drawn from production traffic older than the currently deployed model version.
options.D: Items whose grading requires a model judge rather than a deterministic code check.

items.question: An eval is described as having configuration parity with production. What does that require, and why does it matter?

options.A: The eval must exercise the same prompt version, model, generation settings and surrounding pipeline steps that production uses.
options.B: The eval must run at the same request volume and concurrency as production, so quality effects arising under load appear in the score.
options.C: The eval must grade with the same model that generates in production, so that generation and grading are calibrated against each other.
options.D: The eval must execute inside the production environment itself, since a staging cluster cannot produce outputs comparable to live ones.

items.question: A conveyancing firm is writing the judge prompt for an eval of property-search summaries. The rubric has four criteria and the graded results will be reviewed by the firm's quality partner. Which of the following belong in the judge prompt? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The source search documents the summary was written from, so the judge can check claims against evidence rather than assess plausibility.
options.B: A standing instruction to grade strictly, since judges tend toward leniency and extra severity compensates for that tendency.
options.C: A worked example of an output at each rubric level, together with the reason it sits at that level rather than the next.
options.D: A request that the judge also produce an improved summary, giving the quality partner something actionable alongside each grade.
options.E: A requirement to return an explicit verdict for each of the four criteria, so a failing item is attributable to a named criterion.

items.question: A tour operator's Claude assistant handles multi-turn itinerary-change conversations, averaging six assistant turns per completed change. The eval scores each turn independently against a rubric and reports 93% of turns passing, a figure that has been stable for two quarters. Customers and the contact centre both report that conversations frequently end without the change being made. What should the eval lead change?

options.A: Raise the per-turn acceptance target from 93% to 97%, which will lift six-turn conversation quality into an acceptable range.
options.B: Weight the per-turn pass rate by turn position, since failures late in a conversation damage the customer's impression more than early ones do.
options.C: Make the conversation the unit of evaluation — score whether the change was actually made end to end — and keep per-turn results beneath it.
options.D: Keep per-turn scoring and add a context-retention criterion, since losing context from earlier turns is the usual cause of multi-turn failure.

items.question: A recruitment marketplace uses a Claude step to write candidate summaries for employers. The outcome that matters — whether the employer requested an interview — is known only two to six weeks later. The team needs a signal it can iterate against within a working week, and the head of product has asked for a metric she can put in the quarterly review. How should the eval be designed?

options.A: Use only the delayed interview-outcome labels and accept a six-week feedback cycle, since any faster signal would be an unvalidated proxy.
options.B: Use the model's own predicted interview likelihood as the label, since it is available immediately and is already produced by the system.
options.C: Ask experienced recruiters to predict the outcome when the summary is written and use those predictions as labels until the real outcomes arrive.
options.D: Build a rubric-graded proxy eval on immediately observable properties, and publish how well the proxy tracks the delayed outcomes as they arrive.
